seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Congratulations – or as they put it in your part of the world – I congratulate myself with you on your getting the Dial prize. I hope you are all well. I have been and am rather painfully ill from too much work. I ought to go away for a rest. Best wishes to yourself and family for 1928.

div.note: The face of this postcard shows a photograph captioned “Paris – Le Grand Palais … The Great Palace.” The card was produced by “A Papeghin. – Paris-Tours,” a publisher of collotype postcards, circa 1900-1930, that depicted many views and events, especially in and around Paris. The Grand Palais was built as a vast exhibition hall and museum complex partly fronting the Champs-Élysées, begun in 1897 in preparation for the Universal Exposition of 1900. A contemporary guidebook described its façade as having “a double colonnade, and the building is crowned with low domes. The sculptures of the portal are by Gasq, Boucher, R. Verlet, Lombard, and others. Above the steps at the corners rise two grand quadrigæ (Harmony routing Discord, and Immortality vanquishing Time), by Récipon. Behind the colonnade is a frieze in glass-mosaic, representing the Great Periods of Art, by G. Martin, after E. Fournier. The cupola of the vestibule is richly painted by Besnard. This building is used for the annual exhibitions of the various Salons, for the Concours Hippique, the Salon de l’Automobile, the Concours Agricole (cattle show; Feb.), etc.” (Karl Baedeker, Paris and its Environs [Leipzig: Karl Baedeker, 1924], 70).
The Italian phrase would be something like “Mi congratulo con te.”

The New York magazine The Dial – financed and edited by Scofield Thayer (1889-1982) and further funded by his friend, James Sibley Watson, Jr. (1894-1982) – announced in June 1921 a literary prize to “acknowledge the service to letters of some one of those who have, during the twelvemonth, contributed to its pages by the payment to him of two thousand dollars.” “What we really want to give,” explained Thayer and Watson, “is leisure, leisure through which at least one artist may serve God (or go to the Devil) according to his own lights” (“Announcement,” The Dial, vol. 70, no 6 [June 1921]: 730, 731). The press reported in late December 1927 that Pound was the winner of that year’s Dial Prize (“Dial Prize to Ezra Pound: $2,000 Award is for Distinguished Service to American Letters,” New York Times [26 December 1927]: 23). Other recipients were Sherwood Anderson (1921), T.S. Eliot (1922), Van Wyck Brooks (1923), Marianne Moore (1924), E.E. Cummings (1925), William Carlos Williams (1926), and Kenneth Burke (1928).

The year 1927 had been a trying one for JJ who was laboring away at “Work in Progress” in the teeth of the skepticism of Pound, Harriet Shaw Weaver, and others, and fighting Samuel Roth in a lawsuit an ocean away. JJ had been complaining of exhaustion for months, and wrote two days after this letter that he had “been and am painfully ill – inflammation of intestines – caused by overwork and worry. … I shall really have to go away and rest or I shall have a worse nervous breakdown” (LIII 168). In late January 1928, he was still “recovering” (LIII 169).
